prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock and its development to fractional uncertainties of 10^-18, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Having read the other seven ballots, I move my preferred configuration from my own first choice (B006, cavity method for random constraint satisfaction) to the optical lattice clock (B015). The mechanism is simple and general, which is what I look for: the magic-wavelength condition cancels the light shift so that a very large ensemble of atoms can be interrogated at once, with Doppler and recoil effects removed, and statistical uncertainty drops accordingly. This gives a clean, quantitative physical idea that was then carried to the 10^-18 level by systematic, experimentally controlled work. Four members rank it in their top three, six of eight rank it, and the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed and first realised the lattice clock, and Ye's group brought it to record accuracy and stability and used it for gravitational-redshift tests. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) agree at the 10^-18 level through direct clock comparisons, so the result is not merely that it works but that it has been understood and checked, which matters to me.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is an increment in precision rather than a new principle, and that the 2005 prize (optical frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (control of single ions, with ion clocks) are close. If the citation is written as 'a better clock', the committee will be rewarding degree rather than kind. The case is also partly about what the clocks will do, relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and the redefinition of the second, rather than what they have already shown. Finally, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and Paris groups made essential contributions that a two-name credit cannot reflect. My own B006 remains, in my view, the more universal idea, but it has only one supporter and the Parisi overlap with 2021 is real.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B015 first because lattice clocks improve the best time standard by about two orders of magnitude over caesium, open new ways of observing nature, and are confirmed by multiple independent laboratories; he notes the competition from ion clocks as a possible credit-sharing concern.
responses.response: I agree with the main argument and with the weight on independent confirmation. I would qualify the ion-clock concern: the 2012 prize rewarded control and measurement of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock's decisive step is the opposite one, interrogating many atoms in a magic-wavelength trap so that the signal-to-noise problem is addressed statistically. That is a different mechanism, and the citation should say so explicitly. I would not accept the argument that measurement advances need no further justification, though: the citation should name the mechanism and not only the number 10^-18.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B015 first as precision atomic physics with a simple central idea and large consequences, but warns that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize cover adjacent technology, so the committee must be clear about what is new.
responses.response: This is the point I think decides the matter, and I agree with her framing. I read what is new as the magic-wavelength trapping scheme and the many-atom interrogation it enables, which neither earlier prize covered. I am more cautious than she is about the fundamental-physics payoff: gravitational-redshift tests at the millimetre scale are impressive, but a prize should rest on what has been demonstrated, and I would keep the redefinition of the second out of the citation.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B051 (topological insulators) first as a genuinely new state of matter, and ranks B015 only seventh, saying that it rests on a new level of precision rather than a new principle.
responses.response: I take his objection to B015 seriously and share part of it; it is the main reason I list a reservation above. But I would ask what counts as a new principle: the magic-wavelength condition is one. On B051 I broadly share his view of the physics, since I ranked it sixth and value the simple Z2 mechanism, but I disagree that the allocation is nearly settled. Kane and Mele are one theory partnership, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that guided Molenkamp's experiment, and Zhang is deceased. A trio drawn from the credited names, whether his (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan) or mine (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), leaves out a decisive contributor, so I place it as an alternative and not as my first choice.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino candidate (B040) first as a new observational window, with Halzen as the single credited name, while acknowledging that a sole-laureate prize for a large collaboration may be unfair to AMANDA and other pioneers.
responses.response: I agree that a new window on the universe is a strong criterion, but I am unconvinced that this entry is ready as a prize. The credit is to one person for a collaboration-scale discovery, and the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still at moderate significance, so the interpretation is not yet as settled as the 10^-18 clock comparisons. I would want the committee to understand better who first established the diffuse flux, and I rank it below B015 for that reason. Pearce himself rates the lattice clocks third with strong confirmation, so I hope we can agree they are at least a safe fallback.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B017) first, citing a clean tunable platform and a theory-plus-original-experiment configuration, while acknowledging that the superconducting mechanism is still debated and that recognition may be slightly early.
responses.response: I find the theory-plus-experiment structure of B017 attractive, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction is exactly the kind of simple mechanism I trust. My reservation is the one she names herself: the pairing mechanism and the role of twist-angle disorder are unresolved, so we would be rewarding a platform whose central phenomenon is not yet understood. I would not want to prize something before we know why it works. I therefore prefer B015 now and would revisit B017 in a few years, but I recognise this is a matter of judgement about maturity and not a definitive scientific objection.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or will see it as an increment in precision.
Whether the two-name credit (Katori, Ye) can be defended given the contributions of other clock groups at NIST, PTB and Paris.
Whether the opening strength of B015 reflects the scientific merits or the fact that it is a safe, uncontroversial consensus choice.
I rely on memory for the details of the independent clock comparisons and for the rigorous results behind B006.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B015. I have no known collaboration with Katori or Ye. For B006, my profile shows no link to Mezard or Zecchina, though I work in neighbouring statistical-physics areas. Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson are in the Gothenburg physics environment, but no specific collaboration is recorded.
